blocks.content: This closing topic of the DNS module is a fast, consolidated review of the questions about DNS that come up over and over in real technical interviews, each one pointing back to the full dedicated topic covering it in this module. Treat it as a final self check, if any answer here feels shaky, that is exactly the signal to revisit the full topic behind it.

DNS questions are genuinely common in interviews, precisely because DNS is something almost everyone has heard of but relatively few people can actually explain clearly, step by step. This topic is your chance to make sure you genuinely can.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437673710-18653415.png
1. What Actually Happens When You Type a URL and Hit Enter
blocks.text: 1. What Actually Happens When You Type a URL and Hit Enter

blocks.content: This is very often the opening question in any DNS discussion, precisely because a strong answer requires walking through several connected ideas at once. A DNS lookup happens first, translating the typed domain name into an actual IP address, tying back to the resolution-flow topic full step by step chain. Only once that address is known does the real connection actually begin, everything covered in the Transport Layer and TCP Deep Dive modules.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437673710-484210707.png
blocks.alt: What Actually Happens When You Type a URL and Hit Enter

blocks.content: 2. Recursive Resolver Versus Authoritative Server

Be ready to state this distinction cleanly. A recursive resolver does all the legwork on the requester behalf, following the chain from root server to TLD server to authoritative server, and returning just the final answer. An authoritative server is the one that genuinely holds the real, final answer for a specific domain, everyone else in the chain is just pointing the way there.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437673710-759741871.png
3. What a CNAME Record Actually Is
blocks.text: 3. What a CNAME Record Actually Is

blocks.content: A genuinely common follow up. A CNAME record does not return an IP address directly, it returns another domain name, an alias, which then needs its own separate lookup to finally resolve to a real address. Being able to explain WHY this is useful, one A record update automatically flows through to every CNAME alias pointing at it, shows real understanding, not just memorized terminology.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437673711-390640600.png
blocks.alt: What a CNAME Record Actually Is

blocks.content: 4. Why Caching Is So Important for DNS
blocks.text: 4. Why Caching Is So Important for DNS

blocks.content: Be ready to explain this with real numbers in mind, not just a vague statement. Without caching, every single lookup from every device on the planet would repeat the entire multi step resolution chain, instantly overwhelming the relatively small number of root and TLD servers that the whole system depends on.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437678359-650873185.png
blocks.alt: Why Caching Is So Important for DNS

blocks.content: 5. TTL and the Real Tradeoff It Controls
blocks.text: 5. TTL and the Real Tradeoff It Controls

blocks.content: TTL, time to live, is how many seconds a DNS answer can safely be cached before it needs a fresh lookup. The real tradeoff worth explaining clearly, a long TTL is efficient but slow to reflect a genuine change, a short TTL reflects change quickly but costs more frequent lookups.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437678361-33059334.png
blocks.alt: TTL and the Real Tradeoff It Controls

6. A Deliberately Tricky Follow Up

If a domain IP address just changed, why might some users still be seeing the old site. This tests whether the caching mechanics actually sank in. The answer: those specific users DNS cache, at whatever layer, browser, operating system, or resolver, is still holding an old, not yet expired answer, and will keep using it until its TTL runs out and a fresh lookup finally happens.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437678362-901056204.png

blocks.title: A great follow up to have ready yourself
blocks.content: If asked this, a genuinely strong answer also mentions that this exact scenario is precisely why teams deliberately lower a TTL in advance of a planned migration, directly tying back to the dns-caching topic real world practice.
7. How to Actually Prepare With This Topic
blocks.text: 7. How to Actually Prepare With This Topic

blocks.content: The strongest DNS interview answers consistently explain the WHY behind a mechanism, not just its name. Saying DNS turns names into addresses is a weak, surface level answer. Explaining why caching is structurally necessary, why CNAME records exist, or why TTL represents a genuine engineering tradeoff, shows real, applicable understanding.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437678362-981860171.png
blocks.alt: How to Actually Prepare With This Topic

blocks.title: One habit that reliably improves any DNS answer
blocks.content: Before answering, silently ask yourself, does my answer explain what happens, or does it explain why it happens that way. The second kind of answer is consistently the one that stands out.
8. This Module, Tied Together

This closes the DNS module. Why DNS exists established the motivation, resolution flow walked through the actual multi step lookup mechanics, hierarchy and records covered the structure and the different kinds of answers DNS can provide, and caching explained exactly what makes this entire global system fast enough to actually work at internet scale.

Confusing a recursive resolver with an authoritative server, or a CNAME record with an A record, these specific pairs come up constantly precisely because they are easy to blur together under pressure.
